The commentators explain that the opening words, "Woe to the defrauders," are a warning of ruin and punishment for those who cheat people in measure and weight: when they buy, they take a full and extra amount for themselves, and when they sell, they give less. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn al-Jawzi and Ibn Juzayy note that "wayl" signifies severe harm, ruin or torment. Several, including Ibn Abbas, al-Sudi, al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan, report that it is a valley in Hell where the pus of its people flows, while others take it simply as a general term for severe punishment. There is broad agreement that "tatfif" means short-changing in measuring and weighing, a word derived from "tafif," meaning something slight or small. Some, such as Ibn Atiyya and Ibn Juzayy, extend the sense to any unjust withholding of people's rights.

On the occasion of revelation, most cite the report of Ibn Abbas that the people of Medina were among the worst in measuring, and that they improved after the revelation. Al-Sudi relates the story of Abu Juhayna, who had two measures, one for taking and one for giving. Ibn Kathir considers the surah Medinan, while Ibn al-Qayyim and others regard it as Meccan, and some place it between the two. The commentators agree that the next verses describe people who, when they receive, demand their full due, and when they give, shortchange others. The rhetorical question "Do they not think that they will be raised?" is read as a reproach and an expression of astonishment at their boldness. The "great day" is the Day of Judgment. Regarding "the day when people stand before the Lord of the worlds," opinions differ: Ibn Umar, Ibn Mas'ud, Ka'b and others mention the length of that standing, with reports ranging from a hundred years to three hundred years, forty years, or fifty thousand years, describing sweat rising to the ears. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir understand it as rising from the graves, while al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Atiyya understand it as standing for judgment, and Abu al-Su'ud finds the first meaning the most preferable.

This passage of Surah al-Mutaffifin condemns those who, when they buy from people by measure, demand their full due, yet short-change others when they sell to them by measure or weight. Most commentators explain "wayl" as ruin and severe punishment, while some say it is a valley in Hell. The word "mutaffif" refers to one who diminishes another's right in measuring or weighing, from the root meaning something slight or small. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir take the verse primarily to concern measuring and weighing, whereas al-Sa'di holds that the warning covers anyone who takes people's property by force, and that such a person deserves this warning even more than short-changers do.

The commentators agree that the verse requires fair dealing in trade, and that the rhetorical question "do they not think?" expresses astonishment and condemnation at their boldness in forgetting the Resurrection. The main differences concern the phrase "'ala al-nas". Al-Farra' and al-Zamakhshari hold that "'ala" and "min" are interchangeable here, while Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn Juzayy see in "'ala" a sign of harm and oppression inflicted on people. Scholars also differ over where to pause at "kalluhum": some treat "hum" as an emphatic pronoun, while others take it as the object, and the latter view is generally preferred.

As for the day when people stand before the Lord of the worlds, the commentators relay reports about sweat rising to the ears. They differ on how long this standing lasts: three hundred years according to some, forty years according to others, and one hundred years according to still others. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report these views without firmly choosing between them, and the duration is understood to vary according to each person's condition.

This passage of Surah al-Mutaffifin warns against cheating in measure and weight, namely taking more than one's due in buying and giving less to others when selling. The commentators explain 'wayl' as ruin or severe punishment, and some say it is a valley in Hell. Ibn 'Abbas and Qatada consider the surah Medinan, while Ibn Mas'ud, al-Dahhak and Muqatil call it Meccan, and others say it was revealed between Mecca and Medina. Most understand the following verse as describing their dealings when they sell to people and reduce the measure or weight. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir stress that this is not limited to scales but covers any wrong done to people's rights. The verse then expresses astonishment that they do not think they will be raised up for a tremendous day, when people stand before the Lord of the worlds. Scholars differ on how long this standing lasts: Ibn 'Umar, Ibn Mas'ud and Ka'b give different figures, and a hadith reports that sweat reaches the ears. The commentaries agree on the gravity of this sin and on the importance of fairness in dealings.

This passage of Surat al-Mutaffifin addresses cheating in measure and weight, that is, wronging people of their due by giving less or by taking more unjustly when measuring. The commentators read the phrase "Do they not think that they will be raised again?" as a rhetorical question of rebuke aimed at these cheats: how can they not be certain, or at least consider it likely, that they will be raised for a tremendous day? Al-Tabari, al-Razi, Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Ashur take the word "zann" here to mean certainty, while al-Qurtubi, al-Baghawi and al-Shawkani accept a mere probable belief, since anyone who had even such a belief would hold back from fraud. All agree that the tremendous day is the Day of Resurrection, and that the clause "the day when people stand before the Lord of the worlds" specifies that day or the standing that occurs in it.

To describe that standing, most exegetes cite hadiths from Ibn 'Umar about the sweat rising to the ears, and reports about its length. Al-Tabari gives opinions ranging from a hundred years to three hundred years and more, and others that speak of fifty thousand years, while Ibn Kathir notes that it is made light for believers, to the point of being like an obligatory prayer according to some. Ibn 'Ashur and al-Zamakhshari stress that the greatness of the day and the majesty of the Lord express the gravity of this offence, which is a form of injustice toward others. Several reports attributed to Ibn 'Abbas also mention punishments for those who diminish measure and weight.

This verse speaks of "a tremendous day", the Day of Resurrection when people are raised to be judged. Most commentators, including al-Zamakhshari, Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi and Ibn 'Ashur, read the question "Do they not think…?" as a rebuke and expression of astonishment: the cheats should be certain that they will be raised for a terrible day, and such certainty alone would stop them from cheating. Abu Hayyan, Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn 'Uthaymin take the word "yazunnu" to mean "be certain", while al-Tabari and al-Razi keep its ordinary sense of supposition; al-Razi argues that even a bare suspicion should frighten a sensible person, since divine wisdom would not leave human deeds without account.

The commentators agree that the greatness of the day lies in the terrors and the judgement that take place in it, and that people stand humbly before the Lord of the worlds. On how long this standing lasts, the reports differ: al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi cite opinions of one hundred years, forty years or three hundred years, and al-Tabari adds that it will be lightened for the believer until it lasts no longer than an obligatory prayer. Al-Qurtubi cites a report of fifty thousand years. Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi also note that sweat rises on each person according to his deeds, reaching the bridle of the mouth for some and the middle of the ears for others. Al-Tabari and Ibn 'Ashur see the standing as a state that evokes God's majesty, and Ibn 'Ashur adds that the mention of doubt, the rebuke and the greatness of the day show how grave the sin of short-weighing is.

This verse describes the Day when people will stand before the Lord of the worlds to be judged. It forms part of the warning addressed to those who cheat in measure and weight. The commentators read it as a reminder of resurrection and recompense, and as a picture of the greatness of that Day and of all creation's submission to God. Al-Zamakhshari, Abu al-Su'ud and al-Alusi observe that the mention of the Day's greatness and of God's lordship over all the worlds underlines how grave cheating and injustice are.

The length and manner of this standing vary across the reports. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi cite a hadith transmitted through Ibn Umar that people will stand until the sweat reaches the middle of their ears. Other traditions mention one hundred years, three hundred years or forty years, and some add that the standing will feel as short to the believer as an obligatory prayer, as Ibn Abbas is reported to have said. Ibn Mas'ud, for his part, said the people will remain forty years with their heads raised toward heaven, and no one will speak to them.

On grammar, al-Tabari and al-Zajjaj take "the Day" as an object of "resurrected", while al-Farra' and al-Qurtubi treat it as an apposition to "a great Day". Ibn Juzayy and al-Baghawi also note the option of an implied verb. Several commentators, including Ibn Juzayy, add that the standing will differ from one person to another according to their condition.

This passage states that the matter is not as the wicked imagine: the record of their deeds is kept in a place called Sijjin. The commentators gave several explanations of the word. Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada, Mujahid, al-Dahhak and others say it is the lowest seventh earth, the abode of Iblis and his offspring, or a rock beneath it where the record of the wicked is placed. Ka'b al-Ahbar says it lies beneath the cheek of Iblis, and Wahb calls it the last of Iblis's domain. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report narrations attributed to the Prophet, some of which are judged weak, and Ibn Kathir stresses the sense of a narrow, low place derived from prison. Al-Mawardi, Ibn al-Jawzi and Ibn Juzayy also cite meanings such as abasement, ruin, or a general register of the deeds of devils and sinners, without choosing among them. Al-Zamakhshari takes Sijjin as the proper name of a register of evil. As for the phrase 'a written record', Abu Malik understands it as written, Qatada as marked with a sign of doom, and al-Dahhak as sealed. On the particle kalla, some see a rebuke, others the sense of 'indeed'. The verse goes on to warn those who deny the Day of Judgment, and the commentators identify such deniers as transgressors and sinners. Regarding the 'rust' covering their hearts, al-Hasan and Mujahid explain it as sin upon sin until the heart goes blind, and several cite the hadith of a black spot that grows on the heart. Ibn Kathir and al-Razi link the next verse to being veiled from seeing God on the Day of Resurrection, where scholars diverge: al-Shafi'i and Malik read it as implying that believers will see Him, while the Mu'tazilites take it as deprivation of mercy.

The commentators explain that the phrase "And what will make you know what Sijjin is?" magnifies and alarms: its reality lies beyond anyone's knowledge, and the verse then states that it is a written record. Most agree that Sijjin derives from the root of imprisonment, meaning confinement and narrowness, and that it names a place at the bottom of the earth or beneath the seventh earth, as al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi report. Some take it to be a rock beneath the seventh earth, others a well in Hell, and others a black tree, following transmissions attributed to Ka'b al-Ahbar and others. Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Zayd link it to the souls of the disbelievers. Abu 'Ubayda, al-Akhfash and al-Zajjaj read it as a severe prison, while Ibn 'Abbas and others understand it as loss and disgrace, as 'Ikrima said. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi describe it as a comprehensive register recording the deeds of devils, unbelievers and sinners. As for the "rayn" that covers the hearts, al-Hasan and Mujahid take it to be sin upon sin until the heart goes blind, while al-Zajjaj compares it to rust or a thin cloud. The verse saying that they will be veiled from their Lord is cited by al-Shafi'i and others to affirm that believers will see their Lord, whereas the Mu'tazila read it as deprivation of His mercy and acceptance.

This verse describes the record of the wicked, meaning what is written of their deeds and their fate, which is called a written book, clearly inscribed. The commentators agree that this is an exact register, where nothing is added or removed, and an inscription that is never forgotten or erased, like a mark sewn onto cloth. The word sijjin is explained in several ways. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Razi most often present it as derived from prison, meaning a constricted place and the lowest seventh earth. Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada and Mujahid are among those reporting this view. Mujahid describes it as a rock beneath the seventh earth where the record of the wicked is placed, while Ka'b al-Ahbar places it beneath the limit of Iblis. Others describe a well in Hell. Al-Hasan and 'Ikrima take the word to mean ruin and disgrace. Al-Zajjaj, Abu 'Ubayda and al-Akhfash relate it to confinement, while al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan treat it as a proper name taken from an adjective. Ibn Kathir considers the root of prison the most apt, since the lower one goes the narrower the space becomes. Al-Razi and al-Baghawi debate whether the phrase written book explains sijjin or describes the register of the wicked. The general sense remains that this record is regarded as contemptible and tied to the final destiny of the wicked.

The commentators explain that this verse threatens ruin and punishment on the Day of Resurrection for those who deny the Day of Judgment, meaning those who do not believe in resurrection or accountability. Al-Tabari, al-Mawardi and Ibn 'Atiyya understand the word "wayl" as a threat, a great calamity or a severe punishment, while Ibn Kathir describes it as destruction and perdition. All agree that the verse is a direct warning that continues the preceding passages about the fate of the wicked. Ibn 'Ashur argues that denying the Day of Judgment is the root of transgression and sin, because someone who expects no accounting will not keep the limits set by the law. He holds that the verse primarily addresses the polytheists, but also warns Muslims who cheat in measure that they risk falling into the same condition. Al-Qasimi and Ibn Sa'di note that those who deny this day include the wicked, the hypocrites and the disbelievers. Several commentators, including al-Razi, report narrations about the nature of the register of the wicked without settling between them. Most link this verse to the whole surah, of which it forms the strongest rebuke.

This passage describes those who deny the Day of Judgment as transgressors and sinners who exceed all bounds, and explains that this denial drives them to scorn the truth and to call the verses of the Qur'an fables of the ancients. The commentators connect the verse to the warning against cheats: woe on that day to those who deny resurrection and reckoning. Al-Kalbi and al-Samarqandi say it refers to al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, others to al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, and many take it as general, applying to anyone with these traits. Most explain that the transgressor is one who oversteps the right and indulges his desires, and the sinner one who commits many sins, and they hold that belief in the Last Day is what drives people to righteous deeds, so whoever denies it does not work for it.

Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report that ran is sin upon sin covering the heart, which prevents the denier from accepting the truth. Al-Zamakhshari holds that this rust settles on the heart and overpowers it through persistence in major sins and postponing repentance. Al-Hasan says sin follows sin until the heart dies, and al-Zajjaj compares it to a thin cloud over the heart.

All agree that the verse warns against denying the Day of Judgment and that sins corrupt the heart and turn its owner from guidance. They differ on the following verses about being veiled from the Lord: al-Shafi'i, Malik and most of the Sunni scholars take them as evidence that believers will see their Lord, while the Mu'tazilites, as al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi report, understand the veil as being deprived of God's mercy and honour.

This verse says that only the one who transgresses the limits and commits many sins denies the Day of Judgment, and when Allah's verses are recited to him he calls them the fables of the ancients. Al-Tabari explains that the transgressor is one who oversteps in his speech and disobeys God's command, and the sinner is one who sins against his Lord. Al-Baghawi, Ibn al-Jawzi and Ibn Kathir follow this reading. The word "kalla" then rejects this claim, and the commentators agree that the real cause is "ran", the covering of the hearts by accumulated sins. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi cite the hadith of the black spot that spreads over the heart with each sin, and Hasan al-Basri's view that it is one sin after another until the heart dies. Mujahid likens the heart to a palm that closes with each sin until it is sealed, Ibn 'Abbas speaks of a seal, and al-Zajjaj of rust or a thin cloud. Al-Razi notes that repeated sins form a lasting state of the soul. On the veiling mentioned next, al-Shafi'i, Malik and most Sunni scholars take it as proof that believers will see their Lord, while al-Zamakhshari and the Mu'tazilites explain it as contempt or deprivation of mercy. Most commentators see in the verse a warning of the fire and the rebuke of the disbelievers.

The commentators explain that this verse describes those who deny the Day of Judgment as transgressors and sinners, and that when the verses of the Qur'an are recited to them they say they are merely the fables of the ancients, that is, stories and inventions of the past. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi report that this was the claim of the disbelievers, and that the verse was revealed concerning al-Nadr ibn al-Harith or al-Walid ibn al-Mughira according to some accounts, though its meaning is general. They agree that the word 'kalla' that follows rejects this claim and points to the real cause, namely the veil (ran) that covers their hearts because of their accumulated sins. Al-Hasan, Mujahid, Qatada and Ibn Zayd explain this ran as one sin after another until the heart becomes blind and black; Ibn Abbas understands it as a seal placed upon the heart, and al-Zajjaj compares it to rust or a thin cloud. On the phrase 'they will be veiled from their Lord that day', al-Shafi'i and Malik take it as evidence that the believers will see God, while al-Zamakhshari and the Mu'tazila read it as a humiliation or a denial of divine mercy, and the commentators do not settle between these readings.

The commentators explain that the word "kalla" is a rebuke aimed at the transgressor who claims that the Quranic verses are the fables of the ancients. The following "bal" states the real cause of that claim: "rana" means that sins have overcome and covered the hearts until they are submerged. The root meaning is domination, as wine dominates the mind of a drunkard. The commentators agree that one sin leads to another until the heart is blackened and blinded, so that its owner cannot perceive the truth. Al-Hasan, Mujahid, Qatada and Ibn Zayd support this reading with the hadith transmitted by Abu Hurayra about a black spot that grows with each sin and is polished away by repentance. Al-Tabari and al-Zajjaj describe the rayn as rust or a thin cloud over the heart. Ibn 'Abbas and al-Kalbi take it to mean a sealing of the heart. Mujahid compares the heart to a palm that closes finger by finger with each sin until it is sealed. Ibn al-Qayyim places the rayn between rust and sealing, and then the lock. Al-Shafi'i and Malik cite the verse "they will be veiled from their Lord that day" to argue that believers will see their Lord, while the Mu'tazila read the veil as a loss of mercy. The passage thus establishes that accumulated sins veil the heart from guidance, and that this veil in the hereafter adds to the punishment of the fire and the reproach.

The commentators explain that the verse means the matter is not as the deniers of the Day of Judgment claim: on that day they will be veiled from their Lord, that is, barred from seeing Him and from receiving His honour. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi hold that the veil covers both the vision and the honour of God. Ibn Abbas, Qatada and Ibn Abi Mulayka report that it means being shut out from His mercy and honour, while others confine the veil to the vision alone. All agree that the disbelievers will not behold their Lord, and that the verse describes their punishment: after the reckoning they will burn in Hell, and then they will be told, as a rebuke, that this is what they used to deny.

Many exegetes draw from the wording that believers will see their Lord. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and Ibn Kathir report the argument of Malik and al-Shafi'i, who reasoned that since God veils some out of wrath, others must see Him in good pleasure. The Mu'tazilites, such as al-Jubba'i, Abu Muslim and al-Qadi, read the veil as a withholding of mercy or acceptance. Al-Zamakhshari also sees it as an image of contempt, like those barred from the presence of kings.

The verse also connects with the preceding idea of ran. The commentators agree that it refers to the heart being covered by accumulated sins. Al-Hasan describes it as sin upon sin until the heart dies, and the hadith of the black spot, cited by Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi, illustrates it. Al-Razi and al-Zamakhshari liken it to a rust that covers the heart.

The commentators explain that this verse announces that those who deny the Day of Judgment, having been veiled from their Lord's mercy and favour, will enter the Fire and burn in it, and that they will then be told in reproach that this is the punishment they used to deny. Al-Tabari reads the word "salu" as meaning that they will be brought to the Fire and roasted, while Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Jalalayn take it to mean that they will enter the blaze and remain in it. Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi note that "salī" refers to direct exposure to the heat of the fire with nothing in between. Abu al-Su'ud, Ibn 'Ashur and al-Alusi explain the particle "thumma" as indicating a difference in rank: in their view, being veiled is a greater humiliation than entering the Fire, though al-Alusi adds that for the devoted believers the veil is the harder punishment of all. On the meaning of the veil, al-Tabari concludes that it covers both the sight of God and His honour, while Qatada and Mujahid understand it as deprivation of mercy and grace, and al-Zamakhshari sees it as a picture of contempt. The Mu'tazilites, such as al-Jubba'i, read it as a refusal of mercy. Al-Shafi'i and Malik cite the verse to show that believers will see their Lord, an argument Ibn Kathir and Ibn Sa'di develop from its implicit meaning. Ibn Kathir and Ibn Sa'di also report that sins gradually stain the heart until they cover it, which is what the word "ran" expresses, citing a hadith from Abu Hurayra.

This verse in Surah al-Mutaffifin says that those who deny the Day of Judgment will be veiled from their Lord on that day, will then burn in Hell, and will be told in rebuke: this is what you used to deny. Al-Tabari holds that the veil means both being deprived of God's honour and not seeing Him, since the verse is general and gives no reason to restrict it to one meaning. Al-Hasan and Qatada stress the denial of God's mercy or His regard, while al-Shafi'i and Malik ibn Anas take the verse as proof that the believers will see their Lord, a view Ibn Kathir also endorses. The Mu'tazilites, as al-Razi and al-Zamakhshari report, read the veil as rejection or deprivation of mercy and deny that God can be seen. On the word ran over their hearts, the commentators agree that it means sins piling up until they cover and blind the heart, and Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi cite the hadith of Abu Hurayra about the black spot on the heart. As for the phrase 'it will be said', most take it as a rebuke spoken by the guardians of Hell, though some attribute it to the angels or to the people of Paradise. The commentators thus agree that the verse warns against persisting in sin and that it describes the punishment of the deniers in three stages.

The commentators explain that this verse affirms that the record of the righteous, that is, the believers who fulfil their duties to God and avoid what He has forbidden, is placed in 'Illiyyin, a lofty place or register set against Sijjin, where the record of the wicked is kept. The scholars differ on what 'Illiyyin is. Ibn 'Abbas in one report, al-Dahhak, Qatada and Mujahid take it to be the seventh heaven; Ka'b and Qatada say it is the right pillar of the Throne; al-Dahhak says it is the Lote-tree of the Utmost Boundary; while Ibn 'Abbas in another report, Muqatil and 'Ata' say it is Paradise, or a tablet of green emerald hanging beneath the Throne on which the deeds are written. Al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj treat the word as a plural with no singular of its own, meaning height upon height, whereas al-Tabari holds that it denotes an elevation not lower than the seventh heaven, without fixing its limit. The commentators agree that the inscribed book is a written record and that the near angels who witness it are the angels, some specifying those of each heaven and others Israfil. The majority hold that the righteous enjoy lasting bliss in Paradise, where they drink a sealed wine of pure quality, whose seal is musk, mixed from the spring Tasnim, which the near ones drink unmixed and which is blended for the companions of the right hand. Opinions on the phrase ending in musk vary between mixture, final taste and fragrance.

This verse states that the record of the righteous lies in a lofty place called 'Illiyyun, and the question "and what will make you know what 'Illiyyun is?" is meant to magnify its status. The commentators agree that the word derives from height and elevation, signifying rising upon rising. They differ, however, on the precise place. Ibn 'Abbas, in one report, and Ibn Kathir take it to be Paradise or its highest parts. Ka'b al-Ahbar, Qatada, Mujahid and al-Dahhak identify it with the seventh heaven or the right pillar of the Throne, and al-Dahhak also places it at the Lote-tree of the Utmost Boundary. Al-Hasan understands it as an ascent toward God. Al-Tabari declines to fix a single location, holding only that it cannot be lower than the seventh heaven, while its exact extent is unknown. Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi emphasize the sense of elevation above all. The commentators also agree that the record contains the deeds of the righteous, and that the closest angels witness it, meaning they attend it and bear witness to the security it grants from the Fire and to success in Paradise. Some note that it is written in the believers' favour, in contrast with the record of the wicked in Sijjin. The precise nature of the place is, as several admit, known fully only to God.

The commentators explain that this verse means the record of the righteous, meaning believers who fulfil their duties and avoid what is forbidden, is written and kept in an exalted place called Illiyyin, and that it is inscribed with care and never altered. The angels who are brought near witness it. Opinions differ on what Illiyyin is. Al-Tabari reports that Ibn Abbas, al-Dahhak and Ibn Kathir place it in the heavens, the seventh heaven or near the Throne, while Qatada and Ka'b al-Ahbar place it at the right side of the Throne. Others, including Ibn Abbas in another report, take it to be Paradise, or a green emerald tablet beneath the Throne. Al-Dahhak places it at the Lote Tree of the Utmost Boundary, al-Hasan understands it as ascent towards God, and al-Farra' as height upon height without end. Al-Tabari concludes that it is an elevation whose limit God alone knows, and that it does not fall short of the seventh heaven. As for the word marqum, al-Baghawi and al-Razi take it to mean a writing that contains what God has prepared of honour, while Ibn Kathir sees it as a register of deeds. The commentators agree that those brought near are the angels, and that their witnessing honours the record, as Ibn al-Qayyim notes, comparable to royal decrees witnessed by the great.

This verse states that the record of the righteous, meaning those who were dutiful to God by fulfilling His obligations and avoiding His prohibitions, is kept in an elevated place called 'Illiyyun'. The commentators differ on the exact location. Ibn Abbas, in the most widely cited report, along with al-Dahhak, Mujahid and Qatada, understood it as the seventh heaven; Ka'b and, in one report, Qatada located it at the right pillar of the Throne; al-Dahhak identified it with the Lote-tree of the Utmost Boundary, while Ibn Abbas in another report said it is Paradise. al-Hasan read it as a sense of elevation and ascent toward God. al-Tabari concluded that it denotes a height beyond any known limit, which is not lower than the seventh heaven, relying on the consensus of exegetes. The 'written record' is, for al-Tabari, a document sealed with God's assurance of safety from the Fire and success in Paradise, while al-Mawardi and others take it to be the register of their deeds. As for 'those brought near', most commentators identify them as the angels, namely those of each heaven according to Ibn Abbas and the angels in general according to Ibn Zayd, while Wahb and Ibn Ishaq identify them with Israfil. Opinions differ on whether the witnessing means attendance or testimony to its contents on the Day of Resurrection. All agree that the righteous will enjoy lasting bliss in Paradise.

The commentators explain that this verse states that the righteous, those who fulfilled their duties and avoided what is forbidden, will dwell in a lasting bliss in Paradise that will never end. Most see it as the opposite of the fate of the wicked, who are veiled from their Lord. They then describe this bliss: reclining on couches and gazing at what God has prepared for them, a radiant delight visible on their faces, and a drink of sealed wine whose final taste is musk.

Opinions differ on the meaning of the gazing and the couches. Mujahid, Ikrima and Ibn Abbas understood it as looking at the honours God has prepared, Muqatil as looking at the people of the Fire, while others, including al-Razi and Ibn Kathir, reported that it means seeing the face of God. As for the rahiq, most take it to be pure wine free of adulteration. Ibn Mas'ud understood it as a mixed drink, Mujahid as wine sealed with clay, and Sa'id ibn Jubayr and 'Alqama as wine whose last taste is musk.

Tasnim, according to Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn Abbas, is a spring in Paradise drunk pure by those brought near and mixed for the companions of the right hand; others take it as the name of a drink. The verse, in the general view, calls believers to compete in righteous deeds to attain this bliss.

This verse from Surat al-Mutaffifin describes the bliss of the righteous in Paradise. The commentators explain that they recline on couches, the arara'ik, inside canopied alcoves, gazing at the blessings God has given them, and that the radiance of bliss is visible on their faces. All agree that the raheeq is pure wine, unadulterated, and that it is sealed in its vessels. The meaning of 'its seal is musk' is disputed. Ibn Mas'ud and Mujahid take it to mean that its mixture is musk. Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, 'Alqama and Qatada understand it as the final taste: the drinker finds the scent of musk at the last sip. Others hold that the seal itself is musk, or clay perfumed with musk. Al-Tabari prefers the sense of end and conclusion, since khatm in Arabic signals completion. Ibn Kathir and others report that the righteous drink it, while the closest ones drink it pure from the spring of Tasnim, and it is mixed for the people of the right. The nature of Tasnim is debated: some say it is the highest drink of Paradise, others a spring that flows from above. On the gaze, al-Hasan and Muqatil say it is directed at their enemies in the Fire, others take it as gazing at the blessings, and al-Razi understands it as the vision of God. Al-Tabari preferred the majority reading with the verb taʿrifu and nadra in the accusative.

This passage describes the bliss of the righteous in Paradise. They recline on couches within canopies, looking at what God has granted them of honour, and the radiance of delight shows on their faces. Most commentators understand nadra as brightness, beauty and freshness, though Ibn Shajara takes it as suppleness and vitality, al-Dahhak as whiteness, and 'Ali as a spring in Paradise in which the people wash. Ar-rahiq is taken by the majority, including Mujahid, Qatada, Ibn Zayd and al-Tabari, to mean pure wine, while al-Hasan describes a spring mixed with musk. Ibn Mas'ud explains makhtum as mixed. On the word khitam, Ibn Mas'ud and 'Alqama link it to blending, Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan and Sa'id ibn Jubayr to the final sip whose scent is musk, and Mujahid to the clay that seals the vessel. Al-Tabari prefers the sense of ending and final outcome. Al-Tasnim is, according to Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Mas'ud, a spring from which the near ones drink unmixed while the people of the right hand receive a blend, and Mujahid links it to height. Ibn Kathir and others read the call to compete as an exhortation to good deeds in order to attain this bliss, which al-Tabari understands as eagerness to desire and outstrip others to it.

This passage describes the bliss of the righteous in Paradise. The commentators explain that they recline on couches within canopied chambers, looking upon what God has granted them of honour, and the radiance of delight shows on their faces. On the words "they are given to drink of a pure wine, sealed", most agree that raheeq means pure, unadulterated wine, and many cite Hassan's verse. They differ on "sealed". Ibn Mas'ud, and in one report Mujahid, say it means mixed; Mujahid also says it means sealed with clay over its vessel; others, such as Ibn Abbas, Qatada and Ibn Zayd, take the seal to be the final sip, where one finds a scent of musk. Al-Tabari, weighing these, prefers the sense of the end and outcome of the drink, arguing that the word for seal in Arabic does not properly mean mixing. The two readings of the word for its seal (khitamuhu and khatamuhu) are noted, with the commentators saying they are close in meaning. God then calls people to compete for this bliss, that is to strive eagerly towards obedience, as people covet a precious thing. Finally, Ibn Kathir and the majority say the drink is mixed with tasnim, a spring in Paradise from which the near ones drink pure and which is mixed for the companions of the right.

This passage describes the bliss of the righteous in Paradise: they recline on couches within canopies, gazing at the honour God has given them, and the radiance of delight shows on their faces. They are given to drink a pure wine, the raheeq, which the commentators almost unanimously describe as unadulterated wine, free of any impurity. The phrase "its seal is musk" is explained in several ways. Ibn Mas'ud and Mujahid take it to mean a mixture: the drink is blended with musk. Ibn 'Abbas, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, al-Hasan and al-Nakha'i take it to mean the end: at the last sip the drinker finds the scent of musk. Mujahid adds that the vessels are sealed with musk instead of clay, and al-Tabari supports the sense of ending by noting that the Arabic word for seal also means completion. The reading khatamuhu, attributed to Ali, 'Alqama and al-Kisa'i, carries the same meaning according to al-Farra'. The exhortation "let those who compete compete for this" is taken as a call to desire this good eagerly and to hasten to obedience, or to race in good works. As for tasnim, Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Mas'ud describe it as a spring in Paradise from which the closest ones drink it pure while the people of the right hand receive it mixed, while others understand it as water poured down from above.

This passage describes the bliss of the righteous in Paradise. God says that the drink of the righteous, the sealed wine, is mixed with water from a spring called tasnim, from which the near ones drink pure, unmixed. The commentators agree that tasnim is a spring in Paradise and the loftiest of its drinks, but they differ on the meaning of its name. Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan and Qatada, followed by Ibn Kathir, say the near ones drink it pure while it is mixed for the people of the right hand. Al-Dahhak takes tasnim to mean simply water. Al-Tabari, al-Zamakhshari and Ibn al-Jawzi link the name to height: the spring pours down from above on the inhabitants of Paradise, or flows through the air raised up before filling their vessels. Ibn Zayd reports that it issues from beneath the Throne, and Qatada that it fills their cups without a drop falling to the ground. For the rahiq, most take it to be pure wine free of any adulteration. Mujahid explains the seal as clay, while Ibn Mas'ud, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and others understand that its finish, its last taste, is musk. Most identify the near ones with the foremost believers and the righteous with the people of the right hand, though some hold the two groups to be the same. The passage ends by urging believers to compete in good deeds for this reward, and recalls that the guilty used to laugh at the believers in the world.

This verse describes the blessings of the righteous in Paradise: their drink, al-rahiq, is mixed with water from a spring called tasnim, from which the nearest ones (al-muqarrabun) drink it pure, while it is mixed for the people of the right. The commentators broadly agree that tasnim is the proper name of a spring in Paradise. Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada, Masruq and Mujahid report that the nearest drink it unmixed and that it is blended for all other people of Paradise. Al-Baghawi and Ibn Juzayy distinguish the righteous (ashab al-yamin) from the nearest (al-sabiqun), while others hold that both terms refer to the same group, all who enjoy Paradise. As for the meaning of tasnim, al-Dahhak takes it to be water or the noblest drink, al-Zajjaj and Ibn Qutayba derive it from elevation because it flows from above, and Ibn 'Abbas and others say it is one of the hidden things God has kept for the people of Paradise, with nothing comparable in this world. On grammar, al-Tabari records the views of the Basran and Kufan grammarians: 'ayn is parsed as an accusative of praise, as a circumstantial accusative, or, according to al-Akhfash, as an object of yusqawna; the preposition bi- is taken as superfluous, as meaning min, or as implying being quenched by it. Ibn al-Qayyim and Ibn Juzayy prefer the last reading. Some reports link the following verses to the mockery of Quraysh's leaders toward poor believers such as 'Ammar and Bilal.

This verse states that the guilty, meaning the disbelievers, used to laugh at the believers in this world and mock them. The commentators agree that the target was the leaders of Quraysh such as Abu Jahl, al-Walid ibn al-Mughira and al-As ibn Wa'il, and that the believers mocked were poor Companions such as Ammar, Khabbab, Bilal and Suhayb. Ibn Abbas and others name these figures, while Muqatil and al-Kalbi relate another occasion: Ali ibn Abi Talib passing a group of Muslims who were mocked by hypocrites, a report that al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and al-Qurtubi also cite. The verses then describe their conduct: they winked at the believers as they passed, returned home delighted with their mockery, and called them misguided though they had not been sent to watch over them. On who the subject of the first verbs is, al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya favour the disbelievers, while others allow both readings. The passage ends with the promise that on the Day of Resurrection the believers will laugh at the disbelievers while reclining on couches. Ibn al-Qayyim sees in this a reference to looking upon God, whereas Ibn Kathir and others read it as a direct answer to the mockery. The closing question, whether the disbelievers were repaid, is answered by the commentators with a yes: the verb thawwaba means to be rewarded or requited.

This passage from Surah al-Mutaffifin describes how the disbelievers treated the believers in worldly life: they mocked them and laughed at them, and when they passed by them they winked and signalled to one another with their eyes and eyebrows in derision. When they returned to their families they went back self-satisfied, delighting in mocking the believers. The commentators agree that the guilty were the leaders of Quraysh, such as Abu Jahl, al-Walid ibn al-Mughira and al-As ibn Wa'il, and that the believers were their poorer followers, such as Ammar, Suhayb, Khabbab and Bilal. Al-Wahidi, al-Nasafi and others report a different account connected with Ali, but most focus on the general sense. Ibn Atiyya, Ibn Juzayy and Abu Hayyan allow that the subject of 'passed by' may be the believers, while Ibn Ashur holds that the pronouns can refer to either group. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and al-Zamakhshari explain that their saying 'these are surely astray' means they judged the believers to be misguided, and that the disbelievers were not sent as guardians over the believers' deeds. Ibn Atiyya mentions a view that sees in this verse a call to peaceful coexistence, later abrogated by the verse of the sword. On the Day of Resurrection the situation is reversed: the believers laugh at the disbelievers as they are punished, watching them from their couches, a view reported from Ka'b and Qatada. Al-Tabari and al-Baghawi take the question 'have the disbelievers been requited?' as a real recompense, while al-Razi reads it as irony.

This passage describes how the wrongdoers treated the believers in this life. The commentators explain that the criminals, the leaders of Quraysh such as Abu Jahl, al-Walid ibn al-Mughira and al-As ibn Wa'il, mocked poorer Muslims like 'Ammar, Suhayb, Bilal and Khabbab; when they passed by them they winked and gestured in derision, and when they returned home they went back delighted, taking pleasure in mocking the believers. Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Zayd, as cited by al-Tabari, render 'fakihin' as 'conceited' or 'carefree'; some philologists distinguish 'fakihin' (in luxury) from 'fakihin' (joyful), while others treat them as synonyms like tami' and tama', and Hafs read the word without the alif. The commentators agree that the words 'these people are misguided' express the disdain of the disbelievers, and God denies that the disbelievers were appointed to watch over the believers' deeds. They differ on who is speaking: al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir attribute the words to the disbelievers, while Ibn 'Atiyya considers that the believers may be the speakers. Most exegetes see in the verse the promise that on the Day of Resurrection the believers will laugh at the disbelievers as they watch them being punished, a recompense of the same kind as their own conduct. The question 'have the disbelievers been repaid?' is taken by many as a confirmation or as irony, according to the commentators.

This passage from Surah al-Mutaffifin describes how the guilty, the polytheists of Mecca, behaved toward the believers in the life of this world. They laughed at them and mocked them, winked at one another as they passed by in contempt, and when they returned to their families they came back pleased with themselves, delighting in speaking ill of the believers. Their words "Surely these are astray" mean, according to al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Nasafi and al-Jaza'iri, that they regarded the believers as misguided for following Muhammad ﷺ and giving up worldly pleasures for a reward they could not be sure of. The phrase "they were not sent as guardians over them" means that these sinners were not appointed to watch over the believers' deeds and judge them, since they were charged only with reforming themselves, as al-Tabari, al-Razi and Ibn Juzayy note.

The commentators differ on who the speakers are. Al-Tabari and most exegetes hold that the disbelievers are speaking, while Ibn 'Atiyya reports that it may also be the believers who see the disbelievers and call them astray, and no one settles the question between the two readings.

Most agree that the passage goes on to the Hereafter. According to Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi, a door of Hell is opened for the disbelievers, they rush toward it, but it is shut in their faces, while the believers, reclining on couches, laugh at them. Al-Razi and al-Qurtubi add that this laughter comes from seeing the disbelievers' error exposed and the believers' success.

Al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and al-Qurtubi relate that the mockers were Abu Jahl, al-Walid ibn al-Mughira and al-'As ibn Wa'il, who ridiculed 'Ammar, Suhayb, Khabbab and Bilal. Another report, cited by al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi, mentions the hypocrites mocking 'Ali. On the meaning of "fakihin", Ibn 'Abbas says "pleased with themselves", while others say joyful, carefree, or living in comfort, and Abu Hayyan and the grammarians note that the reading without the alif is also established with a similar meaning.

This passage of Surah al-Mutaffifin, as the commentators explain it, describes the mockery that the wrongdoers directed at the believers during their worldly life. According to most reports, the wrongdoers were the leaders of Quraysh such as Abu Jahl, al-Walid ibn al-Mughira and al-As ibn Wa'il, who laughed at poor believers like Ammar, Suhayb, Khabbab and Bilal, winked at them when they passed by, and, returning home, delighted in talking about them with pride. When they saw them, they called them misguided. The phrase 'wa ma ursiluu 'alayhim hafizin' means that these unbelievers were not appointed to watch over the believers' deeds and judge them, a meaning on which the exegetes broadly agree. They differ on who is meant by the subject of 'ra'awhum': al-Tabari, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Zamakhshari take it to be the unbelievers, while Ibn 'Atiyya reports that some take it to be the believers, and some regard that reading as abrogated by the verse of the sword, a view the majority did not adopt. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Juzayy also suggest the sentence may be part of the unbelievers' own speech, saying that they were not sent to watch over the believers. Al-Zamakhshari also mentions a report that the passage concerns hypocrites and Ali ibn Abi Talib, which Ibn Sa'di and others consider unlikely. On recitation, Hafs reads 'fakihin' without an alif, and al-Farra' holds both forms to be dialectal variants with the same meaning. In the afterlife, the believers will laugh at the unbelievers while they are punished, watching them from couches, as Ibn Kathir and others report from Ka'b and Abu Salih. The passage ends with a rhetorical question: were the unbelievers repaid for what they used to do?

This verse states that on the Day of Resurrection the believers will laugh at the disbelievers, as a requital for what the latter used to do to them in this world by mocking them. The commentators explain that the believers, reclining on couches in bliss, look upon the disbelievers suffering and humiliated after their former pride and power, and they laugh at them. Ibn al-Jawzi, al-Nasafi and al-Shawkani speak of a laughter of satisfaction and fitting recompense, while Ibn Kathir sees it as a response to their laughter in this world. Al-Tabari, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir transmit the report from Ka'b that there are openings between Paradise and Hell through which the people of Paradise look down on their enemies, citing the verse, 'He looked and saw him in the midst of the Blazing Fire.' Abu Salih and others report that the gates of Hell are opened to the disbelievers, who are called to come out, but when they approach, the gates are shut in their faces, and the believers laugh at this.

The exegetes agree that the verse consoles the believers and affirms the justice of the recompense, and that it follows the description of the mockery, winking and remarks the wrongdoers made about the believers. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and Ibn 'Atiyya note that the question 'Have the disbelievers been requited?' is meant as confirmation or irony, and al-Razi considers the ironic reading preferable.

Al-Razi, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Qurtubi report that the verse was revealed about the leaders of Quraysh such as Abu Jahl, al-Walid ibn al-Mughira and al-As ibn Wa'il, and that the believers mocked were 'Ammar, Bilal, Suhayb and Khabbab. Muqatil and al-Kalbi, by contrast, relate a cause involving the hypocrites' mockery of 'Ali. The commentators do not settle between these accounts. Hafs's reading 'fakihin' without the alif is treated by al-Farra' as a variant of the same meaning.

This verse describes the scene of the Hereafter: the believers recline on adorned couches, the arā'ik, inside canopied chambers, gazing at the disbelievers who are being punished, and they laugh at them in return for the mockery the disbelievers directed at them in this world. The commentators offer closely related accounts of this gazing. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi report, on the authority of Ibn 'Abbas, Ka'b, Qatada and al-Dahhak, that between Paradise and Hell there are openings or windows through which the believers look down at the people of the Fire; a door is also opened for the disbelievers toward Paradise, and when they reach it, it is shut in their faces again and again, while the believers laugh at them. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and Abu al-Su'ud transmit the same report. Al-Razi cites the same narration and adds that the believers rejoice to see that their lives in this world were well spent. Ibn 'Atiyya mentions a transparent barrier instead of openings. Muqatil says each inhabitant of Paradise has an aperture through which to watch God's enemies. Most commentators, including al-Razi, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir, understand the gazing to include the blessings prepared for the believers, and Ibn 'Uthaymin adds the vision of God's noble face. As for the question 'Were the disbelievers repaid?', Mujahid takes it to mean 'were they requited', al-Razi sees irony in it, and Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan read it as a rhetorical question affirming the matter to the believers. There is general agreement that the word means recompense, which can be good or evil.

This verse describes the scene of the Day of Resurrection. According to the commentators, the believers, reclining on couches in Paradise, look at the disbelievers in the Fire and laugh at them, in return for the mockery the disbelievers had directed at them in this world. The question «Have the disbelievers not been repaid for what they used to do?» is, for most scholars, a rhetorical question seeking confirmation, and the verb «thuwwiba» means to be rewarded. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi take it to mean that they are repaid for their mockery, and al-Tabari cites Mujahid and Ibn Abbas. Ibn Ashur and al-Zamakhshari see irony here, where the word for reward is used for punishment, a point al-Razi also makes. Qatada, as reported by al-Mawardi, understands it as repayment for what they knew of disbelief, while al-Mawardi himself considers a sense of returning from disbelief, as a reproach. Several scholars, including Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi, report that openings between Paradise and Hell let the believers see the damned, and that the gates of Hell open for the disbelievers and then close on them. Al-Qurtubi and al-Baghawi mention that the occasion of revelation concerns Quraysh leaders, with another tradition naming Ali. Al-Qurtubi and al-Baghawi also note a reading in which the lam of «hal» is assimilated. Ibn Juzayy and Abu Hayyan discuss the grammatical construction. All agree on the essential point: mockery returns upon its perpetrators.
